title: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscaloosa, AL
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscaloosa, AL | CBM & County Seat
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in or around Tuscaloosa, AL? We evaluate parcels near the Oak Grove and Brookwood coalbed methane fields and make a written cash offer.
heroLead: Tuscaloosa is the county seat and sits closest of any city in the county to the productive core of the Black Warrior Basin, which puts real weight behind a well-documented mineral interest here.
intro: As the Tuscaloosa County seat, the city holds the courthouse and probate records for every deed and mineral severance filed in the county, which makes it the natural starting point for title work even when the parcel itself sits well outside city limits. Tuscaloosa is also close enough to the Oak Grove and Brookwood coalbed methane fields, the two fields most associated with productive Black Warrior CBM development, that owners here often hold interests with an actual production history rather than pure speculation.

Whether your interest was severed from University-area land, a family farm on the edge of the city, or acreage bought purely for its minerals, the same first step applies: confirm what you hold and where it sits relative to active units before deciding what it's worth.

sections.heading: Proximity to Oak Grove and Brookwood
paragraphs: The Oak Grove and Brookwood fields, both just south and west of the city, were among the most productive coalbed methane developments in the entire basin during the 1990s and 2000s, targeting the Mary Lee and Pratt coal groups at depths shallow enough to make degasification economical. Parcels within or adjacent to those field boundaries carry meaningfully different value than acreage on the far side of the county, and we check your legal description against the historic and current unit maps before quoting anything.

If your interest has ever produced, even modestly, we'll look at the decline curve on the specific well or unit rather than assuming a flat basin-wide average, since CBM wells in this part of the county have varied widely in how long they've held a plateau before declining.

sections.heading: University growth and old family severances
paragraphs: The University of Alabama's expansion and the general growth of the city over the past several decades has pulled a lot of formerly rural land into development, and in many of those transactions the mineral rights were reserved separately from the surface sale. If your family sold land near Tuscaloosa going back a generation or two, it's worth checking whether that reservation survived, because it often did even when nobody involved remembers it explicitly.

We also see interests that trace to University-adjacent land companies from decades past. Those chains can be more complex to trace, but they're routine work for the Tuscaloosa County Probate Court records, and we handle that research as part of our review.

sections.heading: How we price Tuscaloosa-area interests
paragraphs: For producing interests near Oak Grove or Brookwood, we weigh recent royalty history, remaining reserves as best they can be estimated from public production data, and how the specific well has performed against typical basin decline patterns. For non-producing acreage further from the core, we price against comparable Tuscaloosa County transfers and general trend direction rather than a promised royalty stream.
Either way, you'll get a written offer with the reasoning laid out, so you can compare it against a lease bonus, a competing purchase offer, or simply the option of holding the interest as it stands.

faqs.question: How close does my parcel need to be to Oak Grove or Brookwood to have real value?
faqs.answer: There's no hard cutoff. We check your specific legal description against current and historic unit boundaries and let that determine the answer, rather than relying on distance alone.

faqs.question: My family's records reference a land company that doesn't seem to exist anymore. Can you still trace it?
faqs.answer: Yes. Old land company severances are common in Tuscaloosa County, and we're experienced tracing chains of title through successor entities and the county probate records.

faqs.question: Is a mineral interest near the University campus itself likely to have value?
faqs.answer: Developed, densely built areas near campus rarely see new drilling activity, so those interests are typically valued on historic production or speculative basis rather than current development potential, and we'll tell you clearly which applies to your parcel.

faqs.question: What Tuscaloosa County records do you check before making an offer?
faqs.answer: We review the probate court's deed and mineral records, current state oil and gas permits, and any producing unit filings tied to your legal description before we quote a price.
